html:
On 21 August 1986, Lake Nyos, a crater lake in northwestern Cameroon, suddenly released a huge cloud of carbon dioxide that killed 1,746 people and about 3,500 cattle.

The gas came from magma deep underground. For years it had seeped into the bottom of the lake and stayed dissolved under the weight of the water above, like gas in a closed bottle of soda. Something, perhaps a landslide or cold rain, stirred the layers, and the deep water fizzed out somewhere between 100,000 and 300,000 tons of gas at once. The cloud shot up, then, being heavier than air, rolled down the valleys and smothered villages up to 25 km away. It came in the evening, and many people died where they lay.

Scientists call this a limnic eruption. Only two are on record: this one and the Lake Monoun disaster two years earlier, also in Cameroon. Since 2001 pipes have drawn gas out of the deep water of Lake Nyos so that it cannot build up again.
sum: On 21 August 1986, Lake Nyos, a crater lake in northwestern Cameroon, suddenly released a huge cloud of carbon dioxide that killed 1,746 people and about 3,500 cattle.
